doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Cannonball Adderley's band as inspiration, and George Cables's story
summary: Harper says Cannonball's band, not Blakey's, inspired the Harper Brothers; George Cables told of his sound at a rehearsal.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: It was a great band. Because the first band I had, my brother and myself, the Harper Brothers. Of course me being the drummer, everybody thought more that we patterned this after Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. But the band that I was turned on by was Cannonball’s band.
With Roy McCurdy or with Louis Hayes?

Louis Hayes, Sam Jones. But I mean Roy McCurdy is a good friend. I love that band too. But all the bands were good, but it was just the way that Cannonball played, the way he approached the music. Everything, I mean the dance was in the music. That’s the key. When you heard Cannonball I mean it would get you dancing. The dance was in the music and everything they played sounded fun. It reached you. It hit you in the soul. And it was funny because one of the bands I had later on I remember I had George Cables play with me for quite some time. You know we would talk and tell stories, we’d be on the road driving. And he was telling us a story one time about him getting called to make a rehearsal with Cannonball. And at the time I think he thought well wow, making this rehearsal, I’ll be making the gig. But it was just a rehearsal. But he was telling us that when he played the rehearsal, and I guess they all got there before Cannonball did, and they are playing. And when Cannon came and Cannon started playing he was like, oh shucks. You know he said his sound was so big and he swung so hard, George would say one thing he remembered he says, “man, he don’t even need a band.” Because you know that’s the way Cannon plays, the stuff just swung so hard.

He did. He played like he was, I mean he just played with his personality almost. He just was so erudite and, that was great. Great stuff. What did you learn from people like Betty Carter and Dexter Gordon, that generation. Anything that you can pass on?
